Learned borrowing from Late Latin hemicyclus, from Ancient Greek ἡμι- (hēmi-) + κύκλος (kúklos). By surface analysis, emi- + ciclo.
Borrowed from Late Latin hēmicrānia, from Ancient Greek ἡμικρᾱνίᾰ (hēmikrāníă). Doublet of micragna.
Borrowed from Latin hēmisphaerium, from Ancient Greek ἡμισφαίριον (hēmisphaírion).
From Latin haemorrhoidae, from Ancient Greek αἱμορροΐς (haimorrhoḯs).
From Latin emporium (“market”), from Ancient Greek ἐμπορεῖον (emporeîon), from ἔμπορος (émporos, “marketer”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πόρος (póros, “travel”).
From Latin encliticus, from Ancient Greek ἐγκλιτικός (enklitikós). By surface analysis, enclisi + -ico.
Borrowed from Late Latin encōmium, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐγκώμιον (enkṓmion), neuter form of ἐγκώμιος (enkṓmios), from ἐν (en, “in”) + κῶμος (kômos, “festival, revel”).

parole.significato: A line of verse, containing from ten to sixteen syllables, in which the stress falls on the tenth syllable (in classica…
parole.testo: From Latin hendecasyllabus, from Ancient Greek ἑνδεκᾰσύλλᾰβος (hendekăsúllăbos), from ἕνδεκα (héndeka, “eleven”) + συλλαβή (sullabḗ, “syllable”).
Borrowed from Latin energia, from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (enérgeia).
Borrowed from Latin emphasis, from Ancient Greek ἔμφασις (émphasis), derived from ἐμφαίνω (emphaínō, “to show, present”).
Borrowed from Latin ænigma, from Ancient Greek αἴνιγμα (aínigma).

parole.significato: ennead (grouping or system containing nine objects)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin enneas, from Ancient Greek ἐννεάς (enneás), derived from ἐννέα (ennéa, “nine”).
From Latin enōmotarcha, from Ancient Greek ἐνωμοτάρχης (enōmotárkhēs).
From Late Latin entelechia, from Ancient Greek ἐντελέχεια (entelékheia), coined by Aristotle.

From Late Latin aeōnem (“age, eternity”), from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn), from earlier αἰϝών (aiwṓn), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂oy-u-Hō, derived from *h₂óyu (“long time; lifetime”), derived from the root *h₂ey- (“vital force, life, age, eternity”).
Borrowed from Latin ē̆ōus, from Ancient Greek ἠῷος (ēōîos), ἑῷος (heōîos, “of the east; of the morning”), derived from ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”).
Inherited from Late Latin hēpar (“liver”), from Ancient Greek ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”), from Proto-Hellenic *yékʷər, from Proto-Indo-European *yókʷr̥ (“liver”), derived from the root *Hyekʷ-.
From Latin epicoenus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίκοινος (epíkoinos), based on κοινός (koinós, “common”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin epicy̆clus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίκυκλος (epíkuklos). By surface analysis, epi- + ciclo.
From Latin epicus, from Ancient Greek ἐπικός (epikós). By surface analysis, epos (“an epic”) + -ico (“-ic”, adjective-forming suffix).

From epiglottide, from New Latin epiglottis, from Ancient Greek ἐπιγλωττίς (epiglōttís), derived from γλῶττα (glôtta), variant of γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”). By surface analysis, epiglottid(e) (“epiglottis”) + -ale (“-al”, adjectival derivational suffix).

From Late Latin epiglottidem, from Ancient Greek ἐπιγλωττίς (epiglōttís) derived from γλῶττα (glôtta), variant of γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”). By surface analysis, epi- (“above”, “over”) + glottide (“glottis”).

From Latin epigonī, from Ancient Greek ἐπίγονοι (epígonoi), plural form of ἐπίγονος (epígonos, “offspring, descendant”), from ἐπιγίγνομαι (epigígnomai, “to come after”), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”), from γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “to become”).
Borrowed from Latin epinīcium, from Ancient Greek ἐπινίκιον (epiníkion, “victory ode”), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + νίκη (níkē, “victory”).
Learned borrowing from Latin episcopus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos). Compare the doublet vescovo, an inherited term from the same source.
From Late Latin epistola, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ).
From Late Latin epitaphium, from Ancient Greek ἐπιτάφιος (epitáphios, “relating to a funeral”).

From Latin epithalamium, from Ancient Greek ἐπιθαλάμιον (epithalámion, “bridal song”), neuter form of ἐπιθαλάμιος (epithalámios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + θάλαμος (thálamos, “inner chamber, wedding chamber”).
Borrowed from Late Latin epithesis, from Ancient Greek ἐπίθεσις (epíthesis).
Borrowed from Latin epitheton, from Ancient Greek ἐπίθετον (epítheton).
From Latin epōdos, from Ancient Greek ἐπῳδός (epōidós), from ἐπί (epí, “upon, over, above”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).
With a change in ending, from Late Latin epopta, epoptēs, from Ancient Greek ἐπόπτης (epóptēs).
Borrowed from Latin epos, from Ancient Greek ἔπος (épos).

parole.significato: heptarchy (group of seven states, especially (historical) those in Anglo-Saxon Britain)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin heptarchia, from Ancient Greek ἑπτά (heptá, “hepta-: seven”) + -αρχία (-arkhía, “-archy: rule”). By surface analysis, epta- + -archia.
From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin erēmīta, from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης (erēmítēs).
From Late Latin erēmus, Ancient Greek ἐρῆμος (erêmos)/ἔρημος (lonely, solitary, desert, waste). Doublet of ermo.
Borrowed from Latin haeresis, from Ancient Greek αἵρεσις (haíresis, “choice, system of principles”).
From Medieval Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin hēreticus, haereticus, from Ancient Greek αἱρετικός (hairetikós, “able to choose”).
From Latin ergastŭlum (“penitentiary”), from Ancient Greek ἐργαστήριον (ergastḗrion, “workshop”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese ergástulo.

parole.significato: Erythraean (of or relating to the Erythraean Sea)
parole.testo: From Latin erythraeus (“reddish”), as it was used in Erythraeum mare (“the Erythraean Sea”), from Ancient Greek ἐρυθρός (eruthrós, “red”).

parole.significato: Erythraean (of or relating to Erythrae, Beotia)
parole.testo: From Latin Erythraeus, from Ancient Greek Ἐρυθραῖος (Eruthraîos); morphologically Eritre + -eo.
From Late Latin eremus, erēmus, from Ancient Greek ἔρημος (érēmos, “lonely, solitary, desert, waste”), with preservation of Greek accent over vowel length. Doublet of eremo.
From Latin hexa-, from Ancient Greek ἑξα- (hexa-), from ἕξ (héx, “six”).
From Late Latin hexagōnum, from Ancient Greek ἕξάγωνον (héxágōnon), from ἕξάγωνος (héxágōnos, “six-angled”).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin exarchus, from Ancient Greek ἔξαρχος (éxarkhos), from ἐξ (ex) + ἄρχων (árkhōn).
Borrowed from Late Latin eschara (“scar, scab”), from Ancient Greek ἐσχάρα (eskhára, “hearth, brazier, scab”).
From Latin exedra, from Ancient Greek ἐξέδρα (exédra), derived from ἐξ (ex, “out of”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”).
From Latin exēgēticus, from Ancient Greek ἐξηγητικός (exēgētikós), derived from ἐξηγέομαι (exēgéomai, “I interpret; I explain”).
From Latin oesypum, from Ancient Greek.
From Latin exodus, from Ancient Greek ἔξοδος (éxodos, “expedition, procession, departure”).
From Late Latin exorcizāre, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζειν (exorkízein, “banish an evil spirit; bind by oath”).
Borrowed from Late Latin esōtericus, from Ancient Greek ἐσωτερικός (esōterikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin exōtericus, from Ancient Greek ἐξωτερικός (exōterikós).
Borrowed from Latin oestrus, from Ancient Greek οἶστρος (oîstros, “vehement desire, frenzy”, literally “gadfly”).
From Latin ēta, from Ancient Greek ἦτα (êta), later form of ἧτα (hêta), from Phoenician 𐤇 (ḥ /⁠ḥēt⁠/), whence also heth.
Borrowed from New Latin aethalium, derived from Ancient Greek αἴθαλος (aíthalos, “soot”).

From Latin aetherem (“the upper pure, bright air”), from Ancient Greek αἰθήρ (aithḗr, “upper air”), from αἴθω (aíthō, “to burn, shine”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *h₂eydʰ- (“to ignite, burn”).
From Latin etesiae, from Ancient Greek ἐτησίαι (etēsíai).
From Late Latin ethica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), from ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).
From Latin ēthicus, from Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós).
From Late Latin hecticus, from Ancient Greek ἑκτικός (hektikós).
Borrowed from Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογίᾱ (etumologíā), from ἔτυμον (étumon, “true sense”) + -λογία (-logía).
From Latin etymologus, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμόλογος (etumólogos).
Borrowed from Latin Aethiopem, from Ancient Greek.
Borrowed from Latin aethiopicus, from Ancient Greek Αἰθιοπικός (Aithiopikós). By surface analysis, Etiopia + -ico.
Borrowed from Latin Aetnaeus, from Ancient Greek Αἰτναῖος (Aitnaîos), from Αἴτνη (Aítnē) + -αῖος (-aîos). By surface analysis, Etna + -eo.
Borrowed from Late Latin ethnicus, from Ancient Greek ἐθνῐκός (ethnĭkós).
From Latin aethra, from Ancient Greek αἴθρα (aíthra), akin to αἰθήρ (aithḗr, “air; ether”).
Borrowed from Latin eunuchus, from Ancient Greek εὐνοῦχος (eunoûkhos).
From Latin eurīpus, from Ancient Greek εὔριπος (eúripos).
Borrowed from Latin eurus, from Ancient Greek εὖρος (eûros).

parole.significato: to preach the Gospel, to evangelize
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin evangelizāre, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγελίζω (euangelízō).
Borrowed from Latin euhias, from Ancient Greek εὐιάς (euiás).
From Latin euonymos (Pliny), from Ancient Greek εὐώνυμος (euṓnumos, “lucky”), from εὖ (eû, “good”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).
From New Latin exaeresis, from Ancient Greek ἐξαίρεσῐς (exaíresĭs, “a taking out, an extraction”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek φακός (phakós, “lens”) + χοῖρος (khoîros, “pig”).
From Latin phāsiānus, from Ancient Greek φασιανός (phasianós).
From Latin fagus (“beech”) and Ancient Greek πυρός (purós, “wheat”).
Diminutive of Vulgar Latin *facus, from Latin fascis (“bundle of wood”), or perhaps from Ancient Greek φάκελος (phákelos, “bundle”).
Borrowed from Latin phalangem, from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx, “battle order, array”). See also the related falanga and palanca.

parole.significato: Phalaecean (of or relating to the poet Phalaecus; being hendecasyllabic and consisting of a spondee, a dactyl and three…
parole.testo: From Latin Phalaecēus, from Ancient Greek Φαλαίκειος (Phalaíkeios). By surface analysis, Faleco + -eo.

parole.significato: being hendecasyllabic, and consisting of a spondee, a dactyl, and three trochees (of a verse)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phalaecius, phalaecēus, phaleucius, phalaecus [versus], from Ancient Greek φαλαίκειον [μέτρον] (phalaíkeion [métron]).

From Latin phalaena, from Ancient Greek φάλαινα (phálaina, “moth; whale”). The semantic shift from "whale" to "moth" occurred in Hellenistic Greek, likely due to an analogy between the fluttering movement of a moth's wings and the fins or spout of a whale. Doublet of balena (“whale”)
From Latin phalerae, from Ancient Greek φάλαρα (phálara).
From Latin phallus, from Ancient Greek φαλλός (phallós).
Late Latin famfalūca, from Ancient Greek πομφόλυξ (pomphólux, “air bubble”). Cf. Old French fanfalue (“trifle”), French fanfreluche (“frill”).
From Latin phantasia, from Ancient Greek φαντασία (phantasía).
Borrowed from Latin phantasma, or Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma).
Borrowed from Late Latin phantasticus (“imaginary”), from Ancient Greek φανταστικός (phantastikós).
From Late Latin Pharaōnem (“pharaoh”), from Ancient Greek Φαραώ (Pharaṓ), from Hebrew פַּרְעֹה (par‘ōh), from Egyptian pr:aA (pr-ꜥꜣ, “palace”, “pharaoh”).

parole.significato: pareas, a kind of legendary snake
parole.testo: From a wrong reading of Latin parēas, from Ancient Greek παρείας (pareías).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pharyngem, from Ancient Greek φάρυγξ (phárunx).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (pharmakeía, “the use of drugs”).
From Latin pharus, itself from Ancient Greek Φάρος (Pháros).
Borrowed from Latin Phaeācem, from Ancient Greek Φαίᾱξ (Phaíāx), derived from φαιός (phaiós, “grey”).
From Latin phoenīcopterus, from Ancient Greek φοινῑκόπτερος (phoinīkópteros), from φοῖνιξ (phoînix, “crimson”) + πτερόν (pterón, “feather”); compare the genus name Phoenicopterus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin phaenomenon, from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing appearing to view”).

parole.significato: catafalque (platform to display or convey a coffin)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin feretrum, from Ancient Greek φέρετρον (phéretron).
From New Latin, from Latin Phaethon, from Ancient Greek Φαέθων (Phaéthōn).
From Late Latin philanthrōpia, from Ancient Greek φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpía).

parole.significato: phylum (a rank in the classification of organisms, below kingdom and above class)
parole.testo: From Latin phylum, from Ancient Greek φῦλον (phûlon).
From Latin philolŏgus, from Ancient Greek φιλόλογος (philólogos). By surface analysis, filo- + -logo.
From Latin philosophia, from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía), from φίλος (phílos, “beloved”) + σοφία (sophía, “wisdom”). By surface analysis, filo- + -sofia.
Learned borrowing from Latin philosophicus.
Borrowed from Latin philosophus.
Borrowed from Latin philtrum, from Ancient Greek φίλτρον (phíltron), derived from φιλέω (philéō, “to love; to kiss”).
From Latin phimosis, from Ancient Greek φίμωσις (phímōsis, “muzzling”).
From Latin phȳsētēr, from Ancient Greek φυσητήρ (phusētḗr).
From Latin physicus (“physical”, “natural”), from Ancient Greek φυσικός (phusikós).
From Latin physicus (“physicist”, “naturalist”), from Ancient Greek φυσικός (phusikós).
Learned borrowing from Latin physiognomia, from Ancient Greek φυσιογνωμίᾱ (phusiognōmíā, “physiology”), from φύσις (phúsis, “physique, appearance”) + γνώμη (gnṓmē, “means of knowing”).
From Late Latin phlegma, from Ancient Greek φλέγμα (phlégma, “flame; phlegm”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek φλέως (phléōs, “wool-tufted reed”).
Borrowed from Renaissance Latin flōrilegium, calque of Ancient Greek ἀνθολογία (anthología, “flower-gathering”).
Inherited from Latin phōca f, from Ancient Greek φώκη f (phṓkē). Compare French phoque m.
From Latin Phōcaeus, from Ancient Greek Φωκαῖος (Phōkaîos).
Inherited from Latin fōrma.

parole.significato: to form, create, shape, make, mould/mold
parole.testo: From Latin formāre.
From New Latin phōsphorus, from Ancient Greek φωσφόρος (phōsphóros, “light-bearing”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; nodo incerto nell'albero; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: The origin is uncertain. Possibly a corruption of Latin aphractus, from Ancient Greek ἄφρακτος (áphraktos, “undefended”) (ναῦς (naûs, “ship”)).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin phrenesia, from Latin phrenēsis, from Ancient Greek φρένησις (phrénēsis), derived from φρήν (phrḗn, “mind”).
From Latin fūcus (“drone (male bee)”), cognate with Ancient Greek σφήξ (sphḗx).
Borrowed from Latin galliambus, from Ancient Greek γαλλιαμβικόν (μέτρον) (galliambikón (métron)).
Inherited from Late Latin gamba. Cognate with Sicilian gamma ~ jamma.
From Vulgar Latin gambarus, from Latin gammarus, cammarus, from Ancient Greek κάμμαρος (kámmaros). Cognate with Sicilian gàmmaru~jàmmiru.
Inherited from Late Latin ganathus, from Ancient Greek γνάθος (gnáthos).
Inherited from Latin caryophyllus, caryophyllum, caryophyllon, borrowed from Ancient Greek καρυόφυλλον (karuóphullon). Compare Sicilian garòfalu and Venetan garòfoło.
Inherited from Latin caryophyllus, caryophyllum, caryophyllon, borrowed from Ancient Greek καρυόφυλλον (karuóphullon). Compare Sicilian garòfalu and Venetan garòfoło.

parole.significato: of, from or relating to Gaza
parole.testo: From Latin Gazaeus, itself from Ancient Greek Γαζαῖος (Gazaîos).

parole.significato: the treasury in the temple of Jerusalem
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin gazophylacium, from Ancient Greek γαζοφυλάκιον (gazophulákion).
From Late Latin zēlōsus, from zēlus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”), from ζηλόω (zēlóō, “to emulate, to be jealous”). Compare Spanish celoso, French jaloux.
From Late Latin genealogia, from Ancient Greek γενεαλογία (genealogía), from γενεά (geneá, “generation, descent”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”).
Learned borrowing from Latin genesis, from Ancient Greek γένεσις (génesis). Doublet of gente.
Borrowed from Latin genethliacus, from Ancient Greek γενεθλιακός (genethliakós, “pertaining to a birthday”).
From Latin geōgraphia, from Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía).
Learned borrowing from Latin geōmētrēs, from Ancient Greek γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs).

From Latin geōmetria, from Ancient Greek γεωμετρία (geōmetría, “geometry, land-survey”), from γεωμετρέω (geōmetréō, “to practice or to profess geometry, to measure, to survey land”), from γαία (gaía, “earth, land, country”) + μετρέω (metréō, “to measure, to count”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin hierarcha, from Ancient Greek ἱεράρχης (hierárkhēs, “high priest”).

From Latin hierarchia, from Ancient Greek ἱεραρχία (hierarkhía, “rule of a high priest”), from ἱεράρχης (hierárkhēs, “high priest”), from ἱερεύς (hiereús, “priest”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”) (compare -archia).
From Latin gypsum, from Ancient Greek γύψος (gúpsos).
Inherited from Latin Iēsūs, from Ancient Greek Ἰησοῦς (Iēsoûs), from Biblical Hebrew יֵשׁוּעַ (yēšûaʿ).
From a Vulgar Latin *carilium, *carylium, derived from caryon, from Ancient Greek κάρυον (káruon). Cognate with Spanish garojo.
From Medieval Latin jacintus, from Latin hyacinthus, from Ancient Greek ὑάκινθος (huákinthos, “any of several dark blue flowers; a blue precious stone”).
From Latin ïambus, from Ancient Greek ἴαμβος (íambos).
Learned borrowing from Latin gigās, from Ancient Greek γίγᾱς (gígās, “giant”).
Through Vulgar Latin *jilju, ultimately from Latin lilium, from Ancient Greek λείριον (leírion). Compare, e.g., loglio (“darnel”). Cognate with Sicilian gigghiu.
Borrowed from Latin gynaecēum, from Ancient Greek γυναικεῖον (gunaikeîon), derived from γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”).
From Latin gymnasium, from Ancient Greek γυμνάσιον (gumnásion). Compare Catalan gimnàs, French gymnase, Portuguese ginásio, Spanish gimnasio.
From Latin gȳrus, from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros).
From Latin iūdaicus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαϊκός (Ioudaïkós).
Borrowed from Late Latin iūdaismus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαϊσμός (Ioudaïsmós).
Latinized form of older giudio, from Latin iūdaeus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), from Hebrew יהודי (Yehudi).
From Latin zīzyphus, from Ancient Greek ζίζυφον (zízuphon).
From Latin glaucus, from Ancient Greek γλαυκός (glaukós, “blue-green, blue-grey”).

From glottide, from New Latin glottis, from Ancient Greek γλωττίς (glōttís), derived from γλῶττα (glôtta), variant of γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”). By surface analysis, glottid(e) (“glottis”) + -ale (“-al”, adjectival derivational suffix).
From New Latin glottidem, from Ancient Greek γλωττίς (glōttís) derived from γλῶττα (glôtta), variant of γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”).
Borrowed from Latin gnōmōn, from Ancient Greek γνώμων (gnṓmōn, “indicator”), related to γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to know”) and γνῶσις (gnôsis, “knowledge”).
From Vulgar Latin or Late Latin colfus, colphus, culfus, alteration of colpus, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos). Doublet of colpo.
From Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, gummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi).
Borrowed from Latin Gorgōnem, from Ancient Greek Γοργώ (Gorgṓ), from γοργός (gorgós, “terrible”).

parole.significato: gorgonian, sea whip, sea fan (cnidarian of order Alcyonacea, syn. Gorgonacea)
parole.testo: From New Latin Gorgonia, from Latin Gorgō, from Ancient Greek Γοργώ (Gorgṓ).

parole.significato: to govern, to rule, to control, to manage
parole.testo: From Latin gubernāre, from Ancient Greek κυβερνάω (kubernáō).
Borrowed from Latin graphĭcus, from Ancient Greek γρᾰφῐκός (grăphĭkós).
Borrowed from Latin graphium, from Ancient Greek γραφίον (graphíon), γραφεῖον (grapheîon), derived from γράφω (gráphō, “to write”).
Borrowed from Latin Graius, from Ancient Greek Γραικός (Graikós, “Greek”). Doublet of greco.
Borrowed from Latin grammaticus, from Ancient Greek γρᾰμμᾰτῐκός (grămmătĭkós), from γράμμα, γράμματος (grámma, grámmatos) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós), from γρᾰ́φω (grắphō, “I write”).
From Latin gramma from Ancient Greek γράμμα (grámma, “a twenty-fourth of ounce”).
From Latin Graecus, from Ancient Greek Γραικός (Graikós).
Latin grȳphus, gryps, from Ancient Greek γρύψ (grúps).
From Latin gryllus, from Ancient Greek γρύλλος (grúllos).
From Latin conger (“conger eel”), from Ancient Greek γόγγρος (góngros).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *grupta ~ *crupta, from Latin crypta, from Ancient Greek κρυπτή (kruptḗ). Doublet of cripta, which Italian borrowed from Latin. Found in the toponym Grotte. Compare Sicilian grutta, the probable source of Spanish gruta and Portuguese gruta.
Borrowed from Latin hyalinus, from late Ancient Greek ὑάλινος (huálinos), from ὕαλος (húalos, “glass”).

parole.significato: ancient name of a mineral, probably chalcedony
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iaspidem, from Ancient Greek ἴασπις (íaspis), of possibly Phoenician origin.
From Latin ībis, from Ancient Greek ἶβις (îbis), from Egyptian hbj.
From Latin Latin ibiscum, from Ancient Greek ἰβίσκος (ibískos).
From Medieval Latin īconoclasta, from Ancient Greek εἰκονοκλάστης (eikonoklástēs, “breaker of images”).
Borrowed from Latin Īdalius, derived from Īdalium, from Ancient Greek Ῑ̓δάλιον (Īdálion).
Borrowed from Latin idea, from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”), from εἴδω (eídō, “to see”).

parole.significato: Idaean (of Mount Ida in Crete, especially as an epithet of Zeus)

From Latin nēpenthes, from Ancient Greek νηπενθής (nēpenthḗs, “sorrow-banishing”) (neuter), from νη- (nē-, “not”) + πένθος (pénthos, “grief”).
From Vulgar Latin *nespirum, from Latin mespilum, from Ancient Greek μέσπιλον (méspilon). Compare Portuguese nêspera and Spanish níspero.

From Latin nectar (genitive nectaris), from Ancient Greek νέκταρ (néktar), from Proto-Indo-European *néḱtr̥h₂, derived from the roots *neḱ- (“to perish”) and *terh₂- (“to overcome”).
From Latin nectareus, from Ancient Greek νεκτάρεος (nektáreos). By surface analysis, nettare (“nectar”) + -eo (“-y”, suffix denoting the source of an attribute).
From Latin nīlōticus, from Ancient Greek Νειλωτικός (Neilōtikós).
From Latin nympha or nymphe (“nymph”), from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “young woman, nymph”).
From New Latin nystagmus, from Ancient Greek νυσταγμός (nustagmós, “nodding, drowsiness”), from νυστάζω (nustázō, “nod, be sleepy”).
Inherited from Latin nauclērus, itself from Ancient Greek ναύκληρος (naúklēros).
Inherited from Late Latin naulum (“fare”), from Ancient Greek ναῦλος (naûlos, “a passenger's fee”), from ναῦς (naûs, “ship”).
Borrowed from Late Latin nosocomīum, from Ancient Greek νοσοκομεῖον (nosokomeîon, “hospital”), from νόσος (nósos, “disease, illness”) + κομέω (koméō, “to take care of”).
Borrowed from New Latin nostalgia, coined from Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos, “returning home”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”).
From Late Latin Oasis, from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis), from Demotic Egyptian wḥj, from Egyptian w-H-A-t:N25 (wḥꜣt, “the Oasis region; oasis”).
From Latin obeliscus (“obelisk”), from Ancient Greek ὀβελίσκος (obelískos), diminutive of ὀβελός (obelós, “needle”).
Borrowed from Latin ōceanus, from the name of the deity Ōceanus, from Ancient Greek Ὠκεᾰνός (Ōkeănós).
Borrowed from Latin ōchra, from Ancient Greek ὤχρα (ṓkhra, “pale yellow”).
From Latin ōda, from Ancient Greek ᾠδή (ōidḗ).
Borrowed from New Latin ooecium, derived from Ancient Greek ᾠόν (ōión, “egg”) + οἰκίον (oikíon, “dwelling”).
From New Latin ophiurus (“brittle star”), from Ancient Greek ὄφις (óphis, “serpent”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”) (referring to the serpent-like arms of the brittle star).
From Late Latin oidium, from Ancient Greek ᾠόν (ōión, “egg”).
Borrowed from Late Latin oligarcha, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγάρχης (oligárkhēs). By surface analysis, oligo- (“few”) + -arca (“ruler, leader”).
From Late Latin oligarchia, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχία (oligarkhía). By surface analysis, oligo- (“few”) + -archia (“rule”, “government”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin oligarchicus, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχικός (oligarkhikós). By surface analysis, oligarca (“oligarch”) + -ico (“-ic”, adjective-forming suffix).
From Latin oleum, from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin homileticus, from Ancient Greek ὁμιλητικός (homilētikós, “pertaining to conversation”), derived from ὁμιλέω (homiléō).
Learned borrowing from Latin onagrus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὄναγρος (ónagros, “wild ass”), from ὄνος (ónos, “ass, donkey”) + ᾰ̓́γρῐος (ắgrĭos, “wild”).
From Latin onyx, from Ancient Greek ὄνυχος (ónukhos), from ὄνυξ (ónux, “(finger)nail”).
From Latin oniscus, from Ancient Greek ὀνισκος (oniskos), diminutive of ὄνος (ónos, “donkey, ass”).
From Latin onomatopoeïa.
From Latin onōnis, from Ancient Greek ὀνωνίς (onōnís).
Borrowed from New Latin opisthonephros, derived from Ancient Greek ὄπισθεν (ópisthen, “behind”) + νεφρός (nephrós, “kidney”).
Borrowed from Latin opium, from Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion).

parole.significato: hour (a unit of time of one twenty-fourth of a day (sixty minutes))
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin hōra (“hour”), from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “hour”).
Inherited from Latin aura, from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra, “breeze, soft wind”). Doublet of the borrowing aura.
From Latin Oreadem, from Ancient Greek Ὀρειάς (Oreiás), from ὄρος (óros, “mountain”).
From Late Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”).
Probably borrowed from Latin organum, from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon), derived from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ- (“to make”). Cf. the doublet argano.
From Latin orgia, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὄργια (órgia).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ὄρυξ (órux).
From Latin orīganum, from Ancient Greek ὀρίγανον (oríganon).
From New Latin oryctēropūs, from Ancient Greek ὀρυκτήρ (oruktḗr, “miner, digger”) + πούς (poús, “foot”).
Borrowed from Latin horizontem, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”).

parole.significato: to follow the tracks (of an animal)
parole.testo: From orma + -are, perhaps connected to a Vulgar Latin root *osmāre, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ). Compare Romanian urma.

parole.significato: star-of-Bethlehem, any of various perennial plants of the genus Ornithogalum
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Ornithogalum, itself from Ancient Greek ὀρνῑθόγαλον (ornīthógalon), a compound of ὄρνις (órnis, “bird”) + γάλα (gála, “milk”).
Borrowed from Late Latin hōroscopicus, from Ancient Greek ὡροσκοπικός (hōroskopikós).
From Latin horoscopus, from Ancient Greek ὡροσκόπος (hōroskópos).
Borrowed from Late Latin orthodoxia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθοδοξία (orthodoxía, “right opinion”). By surface analysis, ortodosso + -ia
Borrowed from New Latin osphradium, derived from the root of Ancient Greek ὀσφραίνομαι (osphraínomai, “I perceive a smell”).
From Latin ostrum.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin opticus, from Ancient Greek ὀπτικός (optikós, “of seeing”).
Borrowed from Latin Paphius, from Ancient Greek Πάφιος (Páphios), derived from Πάφος (Páphos, “Paphos”).

parole.significato: any fish of the Pagrus taxonomic genus
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin pagrus, pager, variant of phager, borrowed from Ancient Greek φάγρος (phágros, “sea-bream, braize”).
Derived from Latin pagurus, from Ancient Greek πάγουρος (págouros).

parole.significato: board for use in construction, scaffolding or furniture-making
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin palanca, from Latin phalanga, from the accusative form of Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx, “log, trunk, body of soldiers, etc.”). Doublet of the borrowing falanga and related to falange (“phalanx”).
Probably borrowed from Latin palaestra, from Ancient Greek παλαίστρα (palaístra, “wrestling school”).
From Latin palimpsēstus, from Ancient Greek παλίμψηστος (palímpsēstos, “scraped again”).
Borrowed from Latin Palladius, from Ancient Greek Παλλάδιος (Palládios), derived from Παλλάς (Pallás), epithet of the goddess Athena.

parole.significato: a sculpture or depiction of the goddess Athena
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Palladium, from Ancient Greek Παλλάδιον (Palládion), derived from Παλλάς (Pallás) (see Etymology 1).
Borrowed from New Latin Palladium, named after the asteroid 2 Pallas, named after Ancient Greek Παλλάς (Pallás) (see Etymology 1).
From Latin panacēa, from Ancient Greek πανάκεια (panákeia), from πανακής (panakḗs, “all-healing”), from πᾶν (pân, “all”) + ἄκος (ákos, “cure”).
Borrowed from Latin Pamphylius, from Ancient Greek παμφύλιος (pamphúlios).
Borrowed from Latin panicus, from Ancient Greek πανικός (panikós, “pertaining to Pan”), from Πάν (Pán, “Pan”).
From Latin papa, from Ancient Greek πάππας (páppas).
Learned borrowing from Latin papȳrus, from Ancient Greek πάπῡρος (pápūros).
Borrowed from Latin pappus from Ancient Greek πάππος (páppos), affectionate term for elderly men (referencing beards).
Borrowed from Late Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parola, which was inherited. Mathematical sense taken from New Latin or Greek.
From Late Latin paradīgma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma).
From Latin paradīsus, from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos).
From Latin paraphrasis, from Ancient Greek παράφρασις (paráphrasis).

parole.significato: Any of several species of fish in genus Pagellus
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin pagrus, alternative form of phager, from Ancient Greek φάγρος (phágros).
From Late Latin paragōgē, from Ancient Greek παραγωγή (paragōgḗ, “derivation, addition”).
From Latin paragraphus, from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos, “short stroke in the margin”).
From Latin paralius, from Ancient Greek παράλιος (parálios), derived from παρα- (para-) + ἅλς, ἁλός (háls, halós, “sea”).
From Late Latin paralogismus, from Ancient Greek παραλογισμός (paralogismós).
Borrowed from New Latin, from Ancient Greek παραμήκης (paramḗkēs, “oblong, oval”) + -ium.
From Latin paranymphus, from Ancient Greek παράνυμφος (paránumphos).

parole.significato: the Friday before the Jewish sabbath
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin parasceue, from Ancient Greek παρασκευή (paraskeuḗ, “preparazione”).

From Latin parasītus, from Ancient Greek παράσῑτος (parásītos, “person who eats at the table of another”). Ending reshaped by erroneous analogy with the suffix -ita, from Ancient Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs).
From Latin pardus, from Ancient Greek παρδός (pardós).
From Late Latin parenthesis, from Ancient Greek πᾰρένθεσῐς (părénthesĭs).

From Vulgar Latin *paraula, from Late Latin paravola, from Latin parabola (“comparison; later, speech”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parabola, a borrowing. Compare with French parole, Catalan paraula, Sicilian palora and parola, Spanish palabra.
From Late Latin parochia, from Ancient Greek παροικία (paroikía, “a dwelling abroad”).
Borrowed from Latin Parthus.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin pascua, from Latin pascha (influenced by pascuum, pascua (“grazing”)), from Ancient Greek πάσχα (páskha), ultimately from Hebrew פֶּסַח (pésakh, “Passover”). The surname was given to someone who was born this day.
Inherited from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá).
From Vulgar Latin *pastīcius, from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá).
From Late Latin epitaphium (“eulogy”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιτάφιος (epitáphios, “funereal”).

Borrowed from Late Latin pathēticus, from Ancient Greek παθητικός (pathētikós, “subject to feeling, capable of feeling, impassioned”), from παθητός (pathētós, “one who has suffered, subject to suffering”), from πάσχω (páskhō, “to suffer”).
Probably borrowed from Latin patriarchātus ultimately from Ancient Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs).

From Latin paedagōgus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós).
From Latin pelagicus, from Ancient Greek πελαγικός (pelagikós).

From Latin Pelasgicus, from Ancient Greek Πελασγικός (Pelasgikós), derived from Πελασγίᾱ (Pelasgíā).

From Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ).
From Late Latin pentagonum, from Ancient Greek πεντάγωνον (pentágōnon), from πεντάγωνος (pentágōnos, “five-angled”).
Borrowed from Latin Pentapŏlis, from Ancient Greek Πεντάπολις (Pentápolis). By surface analysis, penta- + -poli.
Borrowed from Late Latin pentarchia, from Ancient Greek πενταρχίᾱ (pentarkhíā), from πεντα- (penta-, “penta-, five”) + -αρχίᾱ (-arkhíā, “-archy, rule”). By surface analysis, penta- + -archia.
From Late Latin pentasyllabus, from Ancient Greek πεντασύλλαβος (pentasúllabos). By surface analysis, penta- + sillabo.
From Latin paeōn, from Ancient Greek παιών (paiṓn), variant of παιάν (paián) (cfr. peana).
Learned borrowing from Latin paeōnia (“peony”), from Ancient Greek παιωνία (paiōnía).

From Latin piper (“pepper”).
Borrowed from Latin peplus, from Ancient Greek πέπλος (péplos).
From Latin perca, from Ancient Greek πέρκη (pérkē, “perch”).

parole.testo: From Latin *percula, diminutive of perca (“perch”).
From Late Latin pergamēna.

From post‐Classical Latin perinaeum (Classical Latin perinaeon), from Ancient Greek περίναιον (perínaion) or περίνεος (períneos), from περί (perí, “around”) with ἰνέω (inéō, “to empty, evacuate”).
Borrowed from Latin periodicus.
From Latin periodus, from Ancient Greek περίοδος (períodos, “circuit, period of time, path around”), from περι- (peri-, “around”) + ὁδός (hodós, “way”).
Inherited from Latin perdīcem (“partridge”), from Ancient Greek πέρδιξ (pérdix, “partridge”).
Borrowed from Latin Persa, Persēs, from Ancient Greek Πέρσης (Pérsēs), from Old Persian 𐎱𐎠𐎼𐎿 (p-a-r-s /⁠Pārsa⁠/, “Persia”).
From Latin persea (“sebesten tree”), from Ancient Greek περσέα (perséa).
From Latin petasus, from Ancient Greek πέτασος (pétasos).

parole.significato: any parsley of the Petroselinum taxonomic genus
parole.testo: From Latin petroselīnum, from Ancient Greek πετροσέλῑνον (petrosélīnon). Doublet of prezzemolo.
From Latin piper (“pepper”), from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi), via Middle Persian from an Indo-Aryan source, ultimately from Sanskrit पिप्पलि (pippali, “long pepper”).
From Vulgar Latin *plattus, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad, flat”). Doublet of chiatto.

Inherited from Latin petra, from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, “stone, rock”).

From Latin, from Ancient Greek πυλωρός (pulōrós, “gatekeeper”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin pilotus, alteration of Latin pedota, from Ancient Greek πηδόν (pēdón, “oar”), from πούς (poús, “foot, leg”).

parole.significato: art gallery, especially one devoted to paintings
parole.testo: From Latin pinacotheca, from Ancient Greek πινακοθήκη (pinakothḗkē). By surface analysis, pinaco- + -teca.

parole.significato: any bird of the genus Pipra
parole.testo: From New Latin Pipra, from Ancient Greek πίπρα (pípra, “kind of woodpecker”).
From Latin pyra, from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr).

Borrowed from Latin pīrāta, from Ancient Greek πειρᾱτής (peirātḗs), derived from πειράω (peiráō, “to try, attempt”).
Borrowed from New Latin pyreticus, from Ancient Greek πυρετικός (puretikós, “febrile”), from πυρετός (puretós, “fever”), from πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).
Borrowed from Latin pȳritēs.
From Vulgar Latin *pisellum, diminutive of Latin pisum, from Ancient Greek πίσον (píson).
From Latin pistacium (possibly through Latin *pistaculum), from Ancient Greek πιστάκιον (pistákion). Of Iranian origin. See also πιστάκη (pistákē).

parole.significato: poultice or medical lotion applied on the chest or belly
parole.testo: From Latin epithema, from Ancient Greek ἐπίθεμα (epíthema, “a cover, column capital, poultice”). Cognate with Spanish bizma.

parole.significato: epithet of the god Apollo; of Pythia
parole.testo: From Latin pȳthius, from Ancient Greek Πῡ́θιος (Pū́thios, “Pythian”).

parole.significato: a member of the Pythium taxonomic genus, of molds.
parole.testo: From New Latin pȳthium, derived from Ancient Greek πῡ́θω (pū́thō, “to (cause to) putrefy”).
Borrowed from New Latin placenta, from Latin placenta (“cake”), from Ancient Greek πλακόεντα (plakóenta, “flat”).
From Latin plasticus, from Ancient Greek πλαστικός (plastikós).

parole.significato: plane, plane tree (tree of the genus Platanus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin platanus, from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos).

parole.significato: stall/orchestra seat (a seat in a theatre/theater close to the stage)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin platēa, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa, “street”). Doublet of piazza.
Borrowed from Late Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós), from πλεονάζω (pleonázō, “I am superfluous”), from πλείων (pleíōn, “more”).
Borrowed from Latin pleuritĭcus, from Ancient Greek πλευριτικός (pleuritikós), from πλευρῖτις (pleurîtis). By surface analysis, pleurite + -ico.
From Latin plinthus, from Ancient Greek πλίνθος (plínthos, “brick”).
From Latin pneumaticus, from Ancient Greek πνευματικός (pneumatikós, “relating to wind or air”), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, air, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “to blow, breathe”).
Borrowed from New Latin podetium, derived from the ποδ- (pod-) stem of Ancient Greek πούς (poús, “foot”).
From Latin poēma, from Ancient Greek ποίημα (poíēma).
Borrowed from Latin poēta, from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs).
From Latin poeticus, from Ancient Greek ποιητικός (poiētikós).
From Latin polemarchus, from Ancient Greek πολέμαρχος (polémarkhos).
From Late Latin polygamia, from Ancient Greek πολυγαμία (polugamía).
From Latin polygamus, from Ancient Greek πολύγαμος (polúgamos).

parole.significato: polygon (plane figure bounded by straight edges)
parole.testo: From Late Latin polygōnum, from Ancient Greek πολύγωνον (polúgōnon).
From [Teucrium] polium, from Late Latin polium, polion, from Ancient Greek πόλιον (pólion), from πολιός (poliós, “white, grey”).
From Latin polīticus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós).
Borrowed from Latin polyptychus, from Ancient Greek πολύπτυχος (polúptukhos, “having many folds”).
From Late Latin polītīa, from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía).
Borrowed from Latin polus, from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos).
From Latin polypus, from Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous). Cognates include Spanish pulpo and Sicilian purpu. Unrelated to polpa.

parole.significato: a sort of polenta made from white flour or fava flour, used as food before the discovery of bread
parole.testo: With a change in ending, from Latin pultem (“meal, porridge”), from Ancient Greek πόλτος (póltos), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”).
Borrowed from Latin pontus, from Ancient Greek πόντος (póntos).
From Latin pornographia, from Ancient Greek πορνογράφος (pornográphos).

parole.significato: pore (of the body, a rock, etc.)
parole.testo: From Latin porus, from Ancient Greek πόρος (póros, “passage”).
From Latin purpura, from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra).
Inherited from Latin pagrus, pager, variant of phager, borrowed from Ancient Greek φάγρος (phágros, “sea-bream, braize”).

parole.significato: to put into practise/practice, to implement
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prāctica (“practical affairs, business”), from Ancient Greek πρᾱκτική (prāktikḗ, “practice, experience”), from πρᾱκτικός (prāktikós, “practical”), from πρᾱ́σσω (prā́ssō, “I do”).

From Late Latin practicus, from Ancient Greek πρᾱκτῐκός (prāktĭkós, “pertaining to an action”), derived from πρᾱγ- (prāg-), the root of πρᾱ́σσω (prā́ssō, “to do”) + -τῐκός (-tĭkós, verbal adjective suffix).
From Late Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros), from πρέσβυς (présbus, “elder, older”).
From Old Italian preite, from Vulgar Latin *previter, from Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros). Compare French prêtre, Romanian preot.

Borrowed from Latin Priamidēs, from Ancient Greek Πριαμίδης (Priamídēs).
Borrowed from Late Latin prisma, from Ancient Greek πρίσμα (prísma), from πρίω (príō, “to saw”).

Borrowed from Late Latin problematicus, from Ancient Greek προβληματικός (problēmatikós), from πρόβλημα (próblēma, “outjutting, barrier, problem”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek πρό (pró, “in place of”) + κύων (kúōn, “dog”).

From Latin prooemium, from Ancient Greek προοίμιον (prooímion).
From Latin prophēticus, from Ancient Greek προφητικός (prophētikós). By surface analysis, profeta + -ico.

parole.significato: a staircase that leads to the entrance of a building
parole.testo: From Late Latin proferulum, itself from Ancient Greek προφερής (propherḗs) + -ulum.
From Latin prognōsis.
From Late Latin programma, from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma).

Borrowed from Latin prognōsticum, from Ancient Greek προγνωστικόν (prognōstikón).
Borrowed from Latin prōra, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πρῷρα (prōîra), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *per- (“to go forth, to cross”). Doublet of proda and prua.
